title: Polar and Euler Form of a Complex Number

resources.title: Resource 1: Theory, Polar Coordinates & Euler's Formula (2.7_content_Eng.pdf)
resources.description: Polar Coordinate System, Definition 2.6, Modulus r and Argument θ, Principal Argument Arg(z) in 4 Quadrants, Euler Formula e^(iθ), and Properties of Products and Quotients

sections.heading: Why Polar Form?
sections.text: Rectangular form (x + iy) is best suited for addition and subtraction. Polar form (r, θ) is best suited for multiplication, division, powers, and roots of complex numbers.

sections.heading: 2.7.1 Polar Form of a Complex Number (Definition 2.6)
sections.text: Let r and θ be the polar coordinates of point P(x, y) representing complex number z = x + iy. Then x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ. Thus: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ), which can also be written in short notation as z = r cis θ.
sections.formula: z = r(cos θ + i sin θ) = r cis θ
sections.notes: r = |z| = √(x² + y²) is the modulus, and θ is the argument or amplitude, written θ = arg(z).

sections.heading: General Argument vs. Principal Argument Arg(z)
sections.text: Since cos θ and sin θ are 2π-periodic, θ has infinitely many values differing by multiples of 2π. The unique value of θ satisfying -π < θ ≤ π is called the principal argument of z, denoted Arg(z).
sections.formula: -π < Arg(z) ≤ π  and  arg(z) = Arg(z) + 2nπ, n ∈ ℤ

sections.heading: 2.7.2 Euler's Form of a Complex Number
sections.text: Euler's formula states that e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ. Therefore, any complex number z can be expressed in Euler's exponential form as z = r e^(iθ).
sections.formula: e^(iθ) = cos θ + i sin θ  =>  z = r e^(iθ)

sections.heading: Properties of Polar Products, Quotients & Inverses

properties.formula: z⁻¹ = (1/r)(cos θ - i sin θ) = (1/r) e^(-iθ)
z₁z₂ = r₁r₂ [cos(θ₁ + θ₂) + i sin(θ₁ + θ₂)], so arg(z₁z₂) = arg(z₁) + arg(z₂)
z₁/z₂ = (r₁/r₂) [cos(θ₁ - θ₂) + i sin(θ₁ - θ₂)], so arg(z₁/z₂) = arg(z₁) - arg(z₂)

items.label: Example 2.22
items.title: Modulus and Principal Argument Across Quadrants
items.problem: Find the modulus and principal argument of: (i) √3 + i, (ii) -√3 + i, (iii) -√3 - i, (iv) √3 - i.
steps: For all cases, r = √((√3)² + 1²) = 2 and α = tan⁻¹(1/√3) = π/6.
(i) √3 + i (Quad I): θ = α = π/6 => Modulus = 2, Arg = π/6
(ii) -√3 + i (Quad II): θ = π - α = π - π/6 = 5π/6 => Modulus = 2, Arg = 5π/6
(iii) -√3 - i (Quad III): θ = α - π = π/6 - π = -5π/6 => Modulus = 2, Arg = -5π/6
(iv) √3 - i (Quad IV): θ = -α = -π/6 => Modulus = 2, Arg = -π/6

items.label: Example 2.23
items.title: Polar Form Representation
items.problem: Represent (i) -1 - i and (ii) 1 + i√3 in polar form.
steps: (ii) 1 + i√3: r = √(1+3) = 2. α = tan⁻¹(√3) = π/3. Quad I => θ = π/3. Polar form: 2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3). General form: 2 [cos(π/3 + 2kπ) + i sin(π/3 + 2kπ)], k ∈ ℤ.

items.label: Example 2.24
items.title: Principal Argument of a Quotient
items.problem: Find the principal argument Arg(z) when z = -2 / (1 + i√3).
steps: arg(z) = arg(-2) - arg(1 + i√3).
arg(-2) = π, and arg(1 + i√3) = π/3.
arg(z) = π - π/3 = 2π/3. Since 2π/3 ∈ (-π, π], Arg(z) = 2π/3.

items.label: Example 2.25
items.title: Product in Rectangular Form
items.problem: Find the product (3/2)(cos π/3 + i sin π/3) · 6(cos 5π/6 + i sin 5π/6) in rectangular form.
steps: Arguments sum: π/3 + 5π/6 = 2π/6 + 5π/6 = 7π/6 = π + π/6.

items.label: Example 2.26
items.title: Quotient in Rectangular Form
items.problem: Find the quotient 2(cos 9π/4 + i sin 9π/4) ÷ 4(cos(-3π/2) + i sin(-3π/2)) in rectangular form.
steps: Moduli: 2/4 = 1/2.
Arguments difference: 9π/4 - (-3π/2) = 9π/4 + 6π/4 = 15π/4 = 4π - π/4 = -π/4.

items.label: Example 2.27
items.title: Locus from Argument Condition
items.problem: If z = x + iy and arg((z - 1)/(z + 1)) = π/2, show that x² + y² = 1.
steps: arg(w) = π/2 implies Real part = 0 and Imaginary part > 0.
Therefore: x² + y² - 1 = 0 => x² + y² = 1 (with y > 0). Proved.

items.label: Question 1
items.problem: Write in polar form: (i) 2 + i2√3, (ii) 3 - i√3, (iii) -2 - i2, (iv) i - 1.

items.label: Question 2
items.problem: Find the rectangular form of: (i) (cos π/6 + i sin π/6)(cos π/12 + i sin π/12), (ii) [cos π/6 - i sin π/6] / [2(cos π/3 + i sin π/3)].
steps: (ii) Numerator = cos(-π/6) + i sin(-π/6). Angle diff = -π/6 - π/3 = -π/2. Result = (1/2)[cos(-π/2) + i sin(-π/2)] = (1/2)[0 - i] = -i/2.

items.label: Question 3
items.problem: If (x₁ + iy₁)(x₂ + iy₂)···(xₙ + iyₙ) = a + ib, show that: (i) (x₁² + y₁²)(x₂² + y₂²)···(xₙ² + yₙ²) = a² + b², (ii) Σ tan⁻¹(yᵣ/xᵣ) = tan⁻¹(b/a) + 2kπ, k ∈ ℤ.
steps: (i) Taking modulus on both sides: |z₁z₂···zₙ| = |a + ib| => |z₁||z₂|···|zₙ| = |a + ib|. Squaring: (x₁² + y₁²)(x₂² + y₂²)···(xₙ² + yₙ²) = a² + b². Proved.
(ii) Taking argument: arg(z₁z₂···zₙ) = arg(a + ib) => arg(z₁) + arg(z₂) + ··· + arg(zₙ) = arg(a + ib) + 2kπ. Since arg(xᵣ + iyᵣ) = tan⁻¹(yᵣ/xᵣ), Σ tan⁻¹(yᵣ/xᵣ) = tan⁻¹(b/a) + 2kπ. Proved.

items.label: Question 4
items.problem: If (1 + z)/(1 - z) = cos 2θ + i sin 2θ, show that z = i tan θ.
steps: Use cos 2θ + i sin 2θ = e^(i2θ) = (cos θ + i sin θ)/(cos θ - i sin θ) = (1 + i tan θ)/(1 - i tan θ).
By componendo-dividendo (or cross-multiplication): [(1+z) - (1-z)] / [(1+z) + (1-z)] = [(1+i tan θ) - (1-i tan θ)] / [(1+i tan θ) + (1-i tan θ)].
2z / 2 = (2i tan θ) / 2 => z = i tan θ. Proved.

items.label: Question 5
items.problem: If cos α + cos β + cos γ = sin α + sin β + sin γ = 0, show that: (i) cos 3α + cos 3β + cos 3γ = 3 cos(α + β + γ), (ii) sin 3α + sin 3β + sin 3γ = 3 sin(α + β + γ).
steps: Let a = e^(iα), b = e^(iβ), c = e^(iγ).
a + b + c = (cos α + cos β + cos γ) + i(sin α + sin β + sin γ) = 0 + i0 = 0.
When a + b + c = 0, we know the algebraic identity a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc.
LHS: (e^(iα))³ + (e^(iβ))³ + (e^(iγ))³ = e^(i3α) + e^(i3β) + e^(i3γ) = (cos 3α + cos 3β + cos 3γ) + i(sin 3α + sin 3β + sin 3γ).
RHS: 3 e^(i(α+β+γ)) = 3 cos(α + β + γ) + 3i sin(α + β + γ).
Equating real and imaginary parts proves both (i) and (ii). Q.E.D.

items.label: Question 6
items.problem: If z = x + iy and arg((z - i)/(z + 2)) = π/4, show that x² + y² + 3x - 3y + 2 = 0.
steps: Numerator = [x(x + 2) + y(y - 1)] + i[(y - 1)(x + 2) - xy] = (x² + 2x + y² - y) + i(xy + 2y - x - 2 - xy) = (x² + y² + 2x - y) + i(2y - x - 2).
arg(w) = π/4 => Im(w) / Re(w) = tan(π/4) = 1 => Im(w) = Re(w).
2y - x - 2 = x² + y² + 2x - y => x² + y² + 3x - 3y + 2 = 0. Proved.
